extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e), 102(f), and 103 (including priority/priority-claim treatment, PCT/international filings, provisional/parent/CIP relationships, and inventorship/derivation issues) during patent examination and for overcoming rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification of references by common ownership / CREATE Act
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) using prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is not proper if the application contains evidence that the application and the prior art reference were owned by the same person, or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, at the time the invention was made; the CREATE Act may treat subject matter developed by another as owned by the same person for obviousness purposes when certain conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies for applications filed on or after Nov. 29, 1999 (or pending on/after Dec. 10, 2004) with respect to 103 rejections relying on 102(e)/(f)/(g) art. 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (as amended by CREATE) applies only to subject matter that qualifies as prior art under 102(e),(f) or (g) and is being relied upon in a 103 rejection; it does not apply to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 or to double patenting. If the subject matter qualifies as prior art under other subsections (e.g., 102(a) or (b)), it will not be disqualified under 103(c). See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)-§706.02(l)(3) for joint research/common ownership procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire disclosure of patent/publication available under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the entire disclosure of a U.S. patent, a U.S. patent application publication, or an international application publication having an earlier effective U.S. filing date can be relied on to reject the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reference is applied as of its earliest effective U.S. filing date (which may include certain international filing dates). See Sun Studs, Inc. v. ATA Equip. Leasing, Inc., 872 F.2d 978 (Fed. Cir. 1989) and MPEP §706.02(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must itself contain the relied-upon subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a U.S. patent, application publication, or international application publication to reject under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the disclosure relied on must be present in the issued patent or application publication itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portions cancelled and not part of the issued patent/published application cannot be relied on (Ex parte Stalego). Subject matter in a parent application but not carried into a child CIP cannot be relied on in a 102(e) rejection over the CIP (In re Lund). For an earlier filing date to be effective under 102(e), the subject matter must be present in the earlier-filed document in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 102(e) references to support 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. patents, and certain application publications/international publications (as of their earliest effective U.S. filing dates), may be used as prior art in 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections by combining them with other prior art to show obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and case law authorize 103 rejections based on 102(e) references (e.g., Hazeltine Research v. Brenner). See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)-§706.02(l)(3) for additional information on 103 rejections that rely on 102(e) art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority dates not usable as 102(e) reference dates
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is limited to references 'filed in the United States before the invention thereof by the applicant'; a reference's foreign priority date (claimed under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d),(f) or 365(a)) cannot be used as a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should not rely on foreign priority dates to antedate an application under 102(e). Applicant may overcome a 102(e) rejection by proving entitlement to an earlier U.S. priority date. See In re Hilmer and MPEP §201.15 for procedures on applicant's right of priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of PCT/international applications for 102(e) purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: An international (PCT) filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e) prior art purposes only if (1) the international filing date is on or after Nov. 29, 2000; (2) the international application designated the U.S.; and (3) it was published in English under PCT Article 21(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all three conditions are met, the international filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e). If not (e.g., did not designate the U.S. or not published in English), do not treat the international filing date as a U.S. filing date; the reference may be applied under 102(a)/(b) as of its publication date or under 102(e) only as of a later U.S. filing date that properly claims its benefit. For international applications filed prior to Nov. 29, 2000, apply pre-AIPA provisions; see MPEP for detailed rules and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional-application priority for 102(e) reference date
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference entitled to the benefit of the filing date of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) has a 102(e) critical date equal to the provisional filing date, provided the provisional properly supports the subject matter relied upon in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706.02(f)(1), examples 5–9. International applications filed before Nov. 29, 2000, or failing to designate the U.S. or be published in English by WIPO, may not be used to reach back to an earlier provisional for 102(e) purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parent application filing date can be 102(e) date only if it supports the relied-upon subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. parent application's filing date is accorded as the 102(e) prior art date for a patent/application publication that claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 only if the earlier-filed parent properly supports the subject matter relied upon in the rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter used in the rejection must be disclosed in the earlier application in compliance with 112(1) to be entitled to the earlier filing date under 102(e). See MPEP §706.02(f)(1) examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(e) reference date is the filing date (not conception/reduction to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: When 102(e) applies (and 102(g) does not), the effective date of the reference as prior art is its filing date in the United States; inventors' conception or reduction-to-practice dates are irrelevant for establishing the 102(e) date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception or reduction to practice become issues only when 102(g) interference is implicated. See Sun Studs v. ATA Equip. Leasing for case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'by another' / different inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is 'by another' when the inventive entity is different from the applicant's; any difference in inventors makes the inventive entity different, and a different inventive entity is prima facie evidence that the reference is 'by another'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharing one or more inventors between the application and the reference is immaterial; the existence of a different inventive entity supports a 102(e) rejection. See In re Land, Ex parte DesOrmeaux, and supporting authorities. See MPEP §706.02(b) and §2136.05 for methods to overcome 102(e) rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection by antedating or showing applicant's work
rubrics_metrics.description: A 102(e) rejection can be overcome by antedating the filing date of the reference (e.g., affidavits/declarations under 37 C.F.R. 1.131) or by showing the relevant disclosure is applicant's own work (affidavit/declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antedating may also be achieved by an earlier foreign priority or provisional application if it supports the claims under 35 U.S.C. 119; a terminal disclaimer does not overcome a 102(e) rejection. See MPEP §706.02(b) for a list of methods and MPEP §§715–716 for requirements of 1.131/1.132 affidavits/declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing the reference describes applicant's own work (derivation/non-prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference actually describes applicant's own invention, the applicant may overcome a prima facie case by showing (e.g., via 37 C.F.R. 1.132) that the patentee or inventors of the reference were associated with applicant and learned of applicant's invention from applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the reference reflects applicant's own work, applicant need not prove diligence or reduction to practice; a declaration of conception predating the reference's filing date may suffice. Case examples: In re Mathews, In re DeBaun, In re Land. Be careful: declarations must be specific; vague disclaimers (e.g., 'not the inventor of the use of the generic compound') may be insufficient (In re Carreira).

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to show diligence/reduction to practice when reference is applicant's own work
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference reflects applicant's own work, applicant need not prove diligence or reduction to practice to establish prior invention; a showing that the reference disclosure arose from applicant's work plus conception before the reference's filing date will overcome the 102(e) rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit an affidavit under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 showing conception and the link to the reference; other patentees' disclaimers may be considered but are not required. See In re DeBaun example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims in a reference do not establish patentee invented individual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere presence of combination claims in a reference is not evidence that the patentee invented the individual elements or subcombinations unless those elements/subcombinations are separately claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re DeBaun and In re Facius: when elements are not separately claimed, inventorship of combination claims does not presumptively show inventorship of the individual elements. This matters when assessing whether a reference was derived from applicant or whether elements were contributed by applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(f) derivation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102(f) applies where it can be shown the applicant 'did not himself invent the subject matter' — i.e., derivation from another; derivation requires complete conception by another and communication of that conception to the alleged deriver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The party alleging derivation need not prove an actual reduction to practice, derivation of public knowledge, or derivation in the U.S. Derivation focuses on originality (who invented) rather than priority (who first invented). Communication must enable one of ordinary skill to construct and operate the invention. See Ex parte Kusko, Scott v. Brandenburger, Kilbey v. Thiele, Price v. Symsek, Hedgewick v. Akers.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(f) may apply where 102(a) and 102(e) are not available
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(f) can be a statutory ground for rejection even when subsections (a) and (e) are not available (e.g., when a reference has an effective date later than the application), because derivation does not depend on relative filing dates alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative dates may still be relevant as evidence of derivation. The standard requires proof of complete conception by another and communication before the alleged deriver possessed knowledge of the invention. Examples and cases illustrate when later-dated references may show derivation from applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requirement and correction procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant for a patent must be the inventor; errors in naming inventors (including where U.S. applications claim foreign priority) must be corrected (e.g., via 37 C.F.R. 1.48(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign applicants must be reminded of U.S. inventorship rules (identity of inventorship between U.S. app and 35 U.S.C. 119 priority application). If the inventive entity named is incorrect and uncontroverted, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) should be made. See MPEP §201.03 and §201.13.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that executor of oath/declaration is inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties executing an oath or declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.63 are presumed to be the inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes about inventorship, absent disagreement, the statements of those executing the declaration are normally accepted as to who are the actual inventors. See Driscoll v. Cebalo and In re DeBaun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must contribute to conception; reduction to practice generally irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: To be an inventor a person must contribute to the conception of the invention; merely suggesting a desired result without the means to accomplish it is not inventorship. Reduction to practice is generally irrelevant to inventorship except in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception is the key inquiry. For chemistry, general knowledge of groups of compounds is insufficient — inventor must have conception of the specific claimed compounds. See In re Hardee, Board of Education v. American Bioscience, and other cited authorities. See MPEP §§2138.04–.05 for evidence required to establish conception or reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor may adopt others' ideas/materials if intellectual domination is maintained
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may adopt ideas, suggestions, and materials from others (employees, consultants, etc.) so long as the inventor maintains intellectual domination over making the invention through testing, selection, and rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of ideas/materials can become a derivation if the inventor fails to maintain intellectual domination. See Morse v. Porter and New England Braiding Co. v. A.W. Chesterton Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication requirement for derivation: sufficiency to enable one skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivation requires communication of a complete conception from the original inventor to the alleged deriver; the communication must be sufficient to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to construct and operate the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high standard: mere mention or incomplete disclosure will not suffice. See Kilbey v. Thiele and cited authorities regarding the level of detail required for a communication to constitute derivation.
